chunks: A number of our companions, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from Ḥammād ibn ʿĪsā, from al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Mukhtār, from al-Ḥārith ibn al-Mughīrah, who said:

Abū Jaʿfar (عليه السلام) said: Indeed, ʿAlī (عليه السلام) was a muḥaddath. So I said: Are you then saying, a Prophet? He said: He motioned with his hand like this, then said: Or like the companion of Sulaymān, or like the companion of Mūsā, or like Dhū al-Qarnayn. Has it not reached you that he said: And among you is one like him?

key_terms.ذِي الْقَرْنَيْنِ: Dhū al-Qarnayn, mentioned as an example of a great servant not identified here as a prophet
key_terms.صَاحِبِ سُلَيْمَانَ: The companion of Sulaymān, cited as an example of a non-prophet granted extraordinary knowledge or support
key_terms.صَاحِبِ مُوسَى: The companion of Mūsā, cited as a parallel figure possessing special divine favor
key_terms.مُحَدَّثًا: One who is addressed or inspired in a special divinely granted manner without necessarily being a prophet
key_terms.مِثْلُهُ: Like him; indicating resemblance in rank or quality being discussed
key_terms.نَبِيٌّ: A prophet; here, the term being explicitly distinguished from مُحَدَّث

ai.seo_question: Does describing Imam ʿAlī (عليه السلام) as مُحَدَّث mean that he was a prophet?
ai.summary: This hadith affirms that Imam ʿAlī (عليه السلام) was مُحَدَّث, meaning one spoken to or inspired, while rejecting that this implies prophethood. The Imam (عليه السلام) clarifies this by comparing him to righteous figures from earlier communities who possessed extraordinary divine support without being prophets.
